text: Okay. Do you see that? Yes, we do. Thank you very much, Reeve. I'm going to make this relatively quick and brief. Though this is an important study for the township and it relates to the finances going forward. And so we were retained by Montague Township to do a development charge study update. The agenda tonight, we're going to talk about the purpose of the development charges, the study methodology, population projections, municipal services, proposed rates, and service allocation, as well as next steps. The key principles for development charge is that it pays for increased capital costs because of increased service needs coming from development. It's based on the concept that growth pays for growth and that taxpayers should not have to pay for growth related capital costs. The same thing is, is that new taxpayers should not have to contribute more than their fair share to the capital costs for their growth related increases. The Development Charges Act requires that a background study be prepared and outline a number of factors, but that the study be prepared and available to the public before council pass a bylaw for development charges. The study that we've done is to determine the eligible development charges that may be collected with growth related capital costs over the next 10 year period. The study was done following the requirements of the Development Charges Act and is intended to conform to the provincial legislation and meets the needs of the township. The study approach we undertook involved a growth forecast based on historic patterns, determination of average level of service that rate payers currently receive in service areas. We've done projections in terms of growth and the elements of growth. We've done calculations based on the type of development, whether it's residential, commercial, or industrial. In terms of the calculations for net growth related capital costs, we have used 2021 present values. We've looked at the net capital costs per person. We've determined household occupancy rates. We've assessed the credits and balances, and we've come up with a charge per residential unit based on the types of units or on the class of land. The township services that we're looking at include general government, which essentially is the funding of the future development charge studies, as well as official plan updates that can get funded through the general development, fire protection services, transportation, and recreation. Those are the four service areas that we've focused on going forward. In terms of population, the 2016 census was the last formal official population count done in the municipality. We have made efforts to project that to the current rate, or the current date, I mean. We've anticipated that there's been slightly less than 300 people added to the population of the township over the last five years. We won't know until February how accurate that number is when the new census figures come out. Using that, however, we were able to make a projection going forward to 2031 from the current position, and we're anticipating over that 10-year period another 300, 310 people being added to the population in Montague. The interesting thing about that is that household sizes are decreasing, and so you actually see more housing units being constructed over that period than population would suggest, but it's because the households are less than 2.5 persons per household. So over the next 10 years, we expect about 310 people to be added to the population count. In terms of development charges that were calculated, the single detached is coming in at around $3,446. Just for your reference, the current rate is $3,248. So the rate we're talking about represents a 6% increase for a single detached house, or roughly $200. One thing is, is the commercial rate is going lower, and that's because there is a lower proportion of commercial industrial development today than what there was previously, and therefore the amount that they're required to pay is less because the demand on commercial industrial is less. It's also worth noting that a number of municipalities do waive the industrial fee, but in this case, it's quite modest. For a 10,000-square-foot industrial building, the development charges would be less than $1,000. Terms of where the development charge money would go if it's collected, roughly 2.5% would go to the general government. That's the studies. About 7% would go to fire protection. The vast majority of the development charge money that's collected goes to roads and public works, and there have been some large reconstruction projects that have been identified for the development charge funds. And then a little less than 10% would go to recreation. In terms of what this means in a financial breakdown for the typical single detached residence, it's about $86 for general eligible, 240 for fire protection, almost $2,800 for transportation, and a little less than $340 for recreation. That's where the money would be allocated to on an annual basis. It's always important to have an appreciation of where your municipality stands in relation to the development charges in other municipalities. I would point out that you're going to be one of the lower DC rates in the county, but you're going to be very close to the Tay Valley rate, the Rideau Lakes rate, or the Drummond North Elmslie rate, albeit slightly less than those, but it is worthwhile to note where you're going to stand. And in terms of the rates that are presented to you in the background report, the council does have the option to adopt the rate as recommended. You can choose to have a lower rate with the understanding that any reduction in development charges has to be picked up by the general rate payers. You could omit certain category rates such as industrial, which is, it happens primarily in the urban centers. They'll do that. And you can deal with exemptions and defined exemptions. At this point in time, that's an option for you, and you can wait until the public meeting and consider this more before you decide what direction you wish to proceed. In terms of going forward, we have published the background report on your website. There's a public meeting that's scheduled for January 20th. And then there's a tentative date for adoption of a development charge by-law at your meeting in February on the 15th, all of which is subject to a 20-day appeal period. Mayor, that is the end of my presentation. If there's any questions that you wish to ask at this time, I'm happy to try and answer them.
